name: Man Mo Temple (Sheung Wan)
summary: Hollywood Road’s historic temple to the civil and martial deities — incense coils under a low timber roof in Sheung Wan.

quickFacts.patron: Man Cheong (God of Literature) & Mo Tai / Kwan Tai (God of War)

body: Man Mo Temple on Hollywood Road is among Hong Kong Island’s oldest surviving Chinese temples, built by local residents in 1847 and managed by Tung Wah Group of Hospitals since 1908. It honours Man Cheong and Mo Tai — the literary and martial deities — and still serves as a working place of worship.
Inside, large incense coils hang above a compact, atmospheric hall. The surrounding Sheung Wan streets mix antique shops and steep lanes; the visit is short but dense with local religious practice.

The coils of incense hanging from the ceiling are paid for by worshippers and can take weeks to burn down. They are the atmosphere of the hall and also the reason the air is thick. The adjacent Lit Shing Kung, for lesser deities, is part of the same Tung Wah complex and is easy to miss if you only photograph the main altar.
highlights: Incense coils and historic temple furnishings
Compact stop on a Sheung Wan / Mid-Levels walk
Free entry; active worship continues daily

visit.intro: Entry is free. The temple is small — expect brief visits and respect ongoing worship.
visit.hours: Typically 8:00am–6:00pm daily; on lunar 1st and 15th and festival days often 7:00am–6:00pm (Tung Wah / TWGHs published hours) — verify before visit.
visit.tickets: Free admission. Incense and offerings are available for purchase on site for worshippers; no ticket is required to enter.
visit.dress: Modest clothing. The hall is compact — backpacks can feel bulky in crowds.
visit.duration: 30–60 minutes including nearby Hollywood Road.
visit.access: Steps and a raised threshold; space inside is limited. TWGHs asks visitors needing assistance to phone ahead (see official temple page).
tips: Address: 124–126 Hollywood Road, Sheung Wan.
Combine with the surrounding heritage streets rather than treating it as a half-day destination.
Smoke from incense can be strong — step outside if needed.
Official reference: Tung Wah Man Mo Temple pages.
Twenty minutes is an honest visit. Combine it with Hollywood Road and the lanes, not with a second temple across the harbour the same hour.
visit.ticketsLabel: TWGHs Man Mo Temple — hours & contacts
visit.ticketsNote: Free entry. Hours per Tung Wah listings — reconfirm before travel.

etiquette.intro: A working temple on a busy tourist street — give worshippers priority.
bullets: Do not block the altar or incense queues for photos.
Keep voices low; remove hats in the hall if customary signs request it.
Ask before photographing people at prayer.
Do not touch plaques, bells, or ritual furnishings.
Follow staff guidance — space is limited.
If the smoke drives you out, leave by the door. Do not wave it away over the altar.

gettingThere.intro: How visitors usually reach Man Mo Temple.
paragraphs: Walk from Sheung Wan or Central MTR along Hollywood Road, or take a tram/bus to the Sheung Wan corridor and continue on foot. The temple sits mid-block at 124–126 Hollywood Road.
Steep side streets connect toward Mid-Levels; wear shoes with grip if you continue uphill after the visit.

Sheung Wan station and the Mid-Levels Escalator are both a short walk. The temple sits mid-block at 124–126 Hollywood Road, set slightly above the pavement. The entrance is easy to pass when a tram is in the way.
bullets: District: Central & Western, Hong Kong Island
Nearest rail: Sheung Wan MTR (then walk)
Phone ahead for accessibility help per TWGHs notice

bestTime.intro: Short visits work best outside festival peaks.
paragraphs: Weekday mornings are usually easier for a quiet look at the coils and altars.
Lunar festival days and deity birthdays bring more worshippers — rewarding if you want atmosphere, slower if you want photos without crowds.
bullets: Avoid lunchtime tour-group surges when possible
Incense smoke is heavier when many coils are lit
Pair with a cooler-season Sheung Wan walk

name: Che Kung Temple (Sha Tin)
location: Sha Tin, New Territories, Hong Kong
summary: Sha Tin’s temple to General Che — wind wheels, incense, and dense crowds on the second day of Chinese New Year.

quickFacts.founded: Origins late Ming; renovated 1890; present main temple built 1994 (CTC)
quickFacts.patron: Che Kung (General Che), Song-dynasty general in local tradition

body: Che Kung Temple in Sha Tin honours Che Kung (General Che), remembered in local tradition as a Song-dynasty general associated with loyalty and protection from epidemic. The Chinese Temples Committee notes origins at the end of the Ming dynasty, a renovation in 1890, and construction of the present larger temple in 1994 in front of the older hall.

It remains a working temple: incense, oracle sticks, and the large fan-bladed wind wheels that worshippers turn for good fortune. The busiest moment of the year is usually the second day of the first lunar month.

The wind wheels in the courtyard are turned by worshippers as a prayer for a change of fortune. Turn one if you are taking part, a few times, and then give it up. Do not hold a wheel so a companion can film you. The drum inside is beaten on festival days for the same reason, under the attendants’ direction, not as a musical instrument.
highlights: Wind wheels and active Taoist / folk worship
Direct access via Che Kung Temple MTR station
Chinese New Year peak (2nd day of 1st lunar month)
Easy half-day pairing with Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery

visit.intro: Entry is free. Festival days — especially early Chinese New Year — require crowd patience, not tickets.
visit.hours: Typically 8:00am–6:00pm daily (Chinese Temples Committee listing) — verify before visit, especially around lunar festivals.
visit.tickets: Free admission. Incense and ritual items may be purchased for worship; no ticket gate for general entry.
visit.dress: Modest clothing. Comfortable shoes; courtyards can be crowded.
visit.duration: 45–90 minutes outside peak festival; longer in queues at Chinese New Year.
visit.access: Generally level temple courts from the MTR approach; expect congestion rather than long climbs. Confirm step-free details on site if needed.
tips: MTR Tuen Ma Line: Che Kung Temple Station, or walk from Tai Wai along Che Kung Miu Road (~10 minutes per CTC).
Four Che Kung festival dates yearly; the 2nd day of the 1st lunar month is the densest.
Turn wind wheels only as local custom and posted guidance allow — do not force past worshippers.
Official reference: Chinese Temples Committee Che Kung Temple (Sha Tin) page.
The second day of the first lunar month is the crowd that defines this temple. Go then only on purpose, and go any other weekday if you want to see the hall.
visit.ticketsLabel: Chinese Temples Committee — Che Kung Temple, Sha Tin
visit.ticketsNote: Free entry. Hours and festival notes per CTC — reconfirm before travel.

etiquette.intro: Respect the tempo of worship — especially when wind wheels and drums draw queues.
bullets: Do not push to the front of offering or wheel lines.
Keep voices low inside halls.
Ask before photographing people at prayer.
Follow attendants during festival crowd control.
Leave ritual objects and offerings untouched.
Festival crowd control is real. A barrier moved by an attendant is not a suggestion you can step around.

gettingThere.intro: How visitors usually reach Che Kung Temple.
paragraphs: The simplest approach is MTR to Che Kung Temple Station (Tuen Ma Line), then a short walk to the temple on Che Kung Miu Road. CTC also notes a roughly ten-minute walk from Tai Wai along Che Kung Miu Road.
Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery is a separate hillside stop near Sha Tin Station — plan walking time if combining both.

Che Kung Temple station on the Tuen Ma Line is the stop named for the building. Leave by the temple exit and walk the short signed path. The walk from Tai Wai along Che Kung Miu Road is the alternative the Chinese Temples Committee describes, about ten minutes, and it is less obvious than the named station.

Tel (CTC listing): 2603 4049
Prefer rail; festival traffic can stall roads

paragraphs: For a calmer look at the halls and wheels, choose a weekday outside the first lunar month rush.
If you specifically want the festival atmosphere, go early on the 2nd day of the 1st lunar month and expect dense crowds — CTC flags this as the busiest date.
bullets: Other Che Kung festival dates: 27th of 3rd lunar month; 6th of 6th; 16th of 8th (CTC)
Summer heat in open courts — carry water
Pair with Ten Thousand Buddhas only if you have energy for stairs later

name: Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery
location: Sha Tin, New Territories, Hong Kong
summary: Sha Tin hillside monastery reached by a long stair lined with golden Buddha statues — free entry, steep approach.

quickFacts.founded: 1950s (founded by Yuet Kai; complex developed mid-20th century)

body: Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery (Man Fat Tsz) rises above Pai Tau Village in Sha Tin. The signature approach is a long outdoor staircase lined with golden Buddha figures in varied poses — a slow climb rather than a flat courtyard visit.

At the top, halls, a pagoda, and terraces overlook the new town. Entry is commonly free; donations are appreciated. The stairs make this a poor choice for visitors with significant mobility limits — plan accordingly.

The golden figures along the stair were commissioned from different makers over the years, which is why the poses do not match. They are offerings lining a monastic approach, not a sculpture park. At the top, the pagoda and the founder’s memorial are devotional spaces: follow the posted rules and do not treat them as a set.
highlights: Hundreds of golden Buddha statues along the ascent
Hilltop halls and pagoda views over Sha Tin
Pair with Che Kung Temple for a Sha Tin sacred half-day

visit.intro: No ticket gate in normal operation — budget time and fitness for the stairs, not admission fees.
visit.hours: Commonly cited as about 9:00am–5:30pm daily — verify on-site or via current visitor notices before travel; last entry may be earlier than closing.
visit.tickets: Entry is typically free; donations welcome. Small stalls may sell incense, drinks, or snacks — prices are separate from admission.
visit.dress: Modest clothing in halls. Closed-toe shoes with grip for uneven steps; avoid smooth soles in rain.
visit.duration: 2–2.5 hours round trip including the climb for most visitors.
visit.access: Steep staircase approach (several hundred steps). Handrails exist on much of the route but steps can be uneven and slippery when wet. Not recommended for visitors with significant mobility or knee difficulties.
tips: MTR East Rail to Sha Tin Station, then walk toward Pai Tau Village and follow signs to the monastery staircase.
Carry water; shade is limited on parts of the climb.
Descend carefully — wet stone is slick.
Hours are less formally published than CTC/TWGHs temples — treat times as verify-before-visit.
Count on several hundred steps and a round trip of about two hours. Chi Lin and Wong Tai Sin are the flat alternatives if the stair is the wrong choice.
visit.ticketsNote: No reliable official e-ticket page; entry typically free with optional donations. Verify hours on arrival or recent local notices.

etiquette.intro: Treat the staircase statues and hilltop halls as part of a living monastery landscape.
bullets: Do not climb on statues or block the stair for long photo sessions.
Keep right when possible so climbers can pass.
Voices low in halls; follow any no-photo signs.
Ask before photographing people at prayer.
Pack out rubbish if bins are full.
Do not pose by hanging off a statue, and do not stop side-by-side on a narrow landing. Climbers need the line.

gettingThere.intro: How visitors usually reach Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery.
paragraphs: Ride the MTR East Rail Line to Sha Tin Station, exit toward Pai Tau, and walk about 10–15 minutes to the base of the monastery stairs. The climb itself often takes 20–30 minutes depending on fitness and stops for photos.
Che Kung Temple is nearby on the same Sha Tin / Tai Wai corridor but is a separate stop — do not assume a single continuous footpath without checking a map.

From Sha Tin station, walk toward Pai Tau Village and the signed foot of the stair. The first five minutes are a village lane; the climb begins once the statues start. Taxis can reach the lane and cannot spare you the steps.
bullets: Area: Pai Tau Village hillside, Sha Tin, New Territories
No cable car — stairs are the main approach
Start earlier in the day so you are not descending at dusk

bestTime.intro: Cooler air and clear mornings make the climb kinder.
paragraphs: Weekday mornings are usually less congested on the stairs. Weekends and holidays can create two-way bottlenecks.
October–April is generally more comfortable than peak summer humidity; after rain, expect slippery steps.
bullets: Avoid midday summer heat on the exposed stair
Carry water and sun protection year-round
Skip the climb during typhoon or black rainstorm signals
Weekday mornings beat Sundays, when the stair becomes two slow queues passing each other.

name: Western Wall
summary: The Herodian retaining wall of the Temple Mount — Judaism’s most visited prayer place, open around the clock and free to approach.

quickFacts.typicalVisit: 45–90 minutes; longer with a tunnel tour

body: The Western Wall (the Kotel) is the western retaining wall of the Temple Mount platform in Jerusalem’s Old City. It is not the Temple itself. For Jewish worship it is the closest openly accessible place to the site of the former Temple, and people come at every hour to pray, to leave written notes in the stones, and to mark family occasions.

The outdoor prayer plaza is free and does not require a ticket. Men and women pray in separate sections of the main plaza. A mixed section, Ezrat Yisrael, is at the southern end of the wall and is a different space from the main men’s and women’s sections.

The Western Wall Tunnels, along the buried continuation of the wall, are a separate visit run by the Western Wall Heritage Foundation. Those tours are timed and ticketed. They are not included in a walk up to the plaza.
highlights: Free prayer plaza, open day and night
Separate men’s and women’s sections, plus Ezrat Yisrael to the south
Tunnel tours booked only via the Western Wall Heritage Foundation
Security screening at the Old City approaches

visit.intro: Plan the plaza and the tunnels as two different visits. The plaza needs no ticket; the tunnels do, and they sell out.
visit.hours: The prayer plaza is open at all hours, with heavier crowds on Friday evening, Shabbat, and Jewish festivals. Tunnel tours run on published slots — check the Heritage Foundation for the week you are travelling.
visit.tickets: No ticket and no booking for the outdoor plaza. Tunnel tours, the Chain of Generations exhibit, and related sites are paid and timed. Buy them only on thekotel.org or tickets.thekotel.org.
visit.dress: Shoulders covered. Men cover their heads at the wall; paper kippahs are usually available at the entrance. Women should dress modestly. On Shabbat, many people avoid photography — follow the attendants rather than the most casual visitor.
visit.duration: 45–90 minutes for the plaza and a slow look at the stones. A tunnel tour adds about an hour and must be booked.
visit.access: The plaza is mostly level once you are through security, with some slopes in the Old City lanes on the way in. Tunnel routes include stairs and narrow passages and are a poor fit for limited mobility.
tips: Use Dung Gate or the Jewish Quarter lanes; allow time for airport-style security.
Write a note if you wish, but do not climb the stones or wedge anything other than paper into the cracks.
Book tunnel tours in advance on the official site, especially in English.
Friday evening and Saturday are for prayer, not a quick photo stop.
visit.ticketsNote: The prayer plaza is free. Tunnel tours are a separate paid ticket on the Heritage Foundation’s own site (tickets.thekotel.org). Do not buy them from street sellers.

etiquette.intro: This is an active place of prayer. Sightseeing gives way to people who are davening.
bullets: Stay quiet. Phone calls and group talks belong back in the lanes.
Do not walk between a person and the wall while they are praying.
Use the men’s section, the women’s section, or Ezrat Yisrael as each is signed — do not cross the dividers.
Ask before photographing individuals, especially on Shabbat and festivals.
Notes left in the wall are prayers, not souvenirs. Do not pull them out.

gettingThere.intro: The Wall sits inside the Old City. The last metres are on foot after a security check.
paragraphs: Most visitors enter near Dung Gate, below the Jewish Quarter. From the Jaffa Gate or the Western Wall light-rail area, follow signs for the Kotel rather than a shortcut through residential courtyards.
There is no parking at the plaza. Use public transit, a taxi to an Old City gate, or walk. On Shabbat many buses do not run and the surrounding streets are closed to cars.
bullets: Light rail or taxi to a gate, then walk through security
Dung Gate is the usual last approach
Do not plan a tunnel tour for Friday afternoon or Saturday unless the official calendar shows a slot
Pair with the Jewish Quarter; the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount above the wall has its own, separate access rules

bestTime.intro: Come when you can stand at the stones without treating a prayer service as a backdrop.
paragraphs: Weekday mornings are the calmest. Bar and bat mitzvah celebrations are common on Monday and Thursday mornings and on Shabbat; they are moving and they fill the plaza.
Friday before sunset the plaza fills for Shabbat. If you are not there to pray, go earlier in the day.
bullets: Calmest: weekday mornings
Crowded: Friday evening, Shabbat, and pilgrimage festivals
Tunnel-tour calendars close on Shabbat and Jewish holidays — read the official week, not a blog

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: The Wall is the retaining wall of the Temple Mount, not a reconstructed Temple. A visit is prayer or quiet looking, not a rite of rebuilding.
Non-Muslim access to the compound above the wall changes often and is a different visit from the plaza. Read the Dome of the Rock guide and check same-day rules.
Security staff can turn bags and large liquids away. Travel light.
Tunnel tickets bought outside the Heritage Foundation are a common scam.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Mahabodhi Temple
summary: The brick temple and Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, where Buddhist tradition places the Buddha’s enlightenment — a living pilgrimage complex, usually without a tourist ticket.

quickFacts.founded: Gupta-period brick temple; much older sacred site

body: The Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya marks the place where Buddhist tradition remembers the Buddha’s enlightenment under a Bodhi tree. The tall brick shrine, largely a Gupta-period form with later restoration, stands beside the tree inside a compound of smaller stupas, railings, and meditation grounds.

The tree in the compound is venerated as a successor of that Bodhi tree, not as a museum object. Monks, nuns, and lay people from many countries sit, walk, and chant here through the day. The Bodh Gaya Temple Management Committee publishes the shrine’s hours: the main shrine opens early morning and closes at night, with chanting at set times.
Treat the visit as pilgrimage first. Shoes come off, voices drop, and the clockwise walk around the temple is the point — not a dash to the tower for a photograph.
highlights: Bodhi tree, temple tower, and circumambulation path
Main shrine typically free of a tourist ticket
Security screening — confirm the day’s phone and camera rule

visit.intro: The committee’s own site is the source for hours. Do not buy a “Mahabodhi entry ticket” from a tout.
visit.hours: The Bodh Gaya Temple Management Committee lists the main shrine as open daily from about 5:00am to 9:00pm, with chanting in the early morning and evening. Outlying spots in the wider town keep different hours.
visit.tickets: The temple committee does not sell a general tourist ticket for the shrine. Security is still real: bags may be searched, and phones or cameras are sometimes restricted. Follow the gate you actually reach, not a forum post.
visit.dress: Cover shoulders and knees. Clothes you can sit in are more useful than clothes that only photograph well. Shoes and socks come off before the inner paths; carry them in a bag.
visit.duration: Two to three hours if you sit as well as walk. A full day if you add the monasteries of different countries along the outer lanes.
visit.access: Paths inside the compound are mostly flat, with some steps at the temple base. The inner shrine can be crowded at chanting times. Ask staff about step-free routes rather than assuming every threshold is level.
tips: Walk clockwise around the temple if you are joining the circumambulation.
Sit only where meditation is clearly welcome; do not block the tree enclosure.
Use a licensed prepaid taxi from Gaya Airport or Gaya Junction.
Recheck bodhgayatemple.com the week you travel — festival calendars add crowds and can shift routines.
visit.ticketsNote: Official committee site for shrine hours. Entry to the main shrine is not a paid tourist ticket. Ignore anyone selling one.

etiquette.intro: People are meditating. A camera is not a reason to step over them.
bullets: Silence phones. If a call is unavoidable, leave the inner compound.
Do not touch the tree, the railing around it, or offerings.
Do not sit on statues, vajrasana, or the lotus plinths.
Ask before photographing monastics or anyone at prayer.
Chanting sessions are worship. Stay at the edge unless you have been invited in.

gettingThere.intro: Bodh Gaya is a small town. The temple is the centre, and the airport and railway are both a short drive away.
paragraphs: Gaya Airport (GAY) and Gaya Junction are the usual arrivals. The temple is a prepaid-taxi ride, not a walk from either. Bodh Gaya’s outer roads are lined with monasteries — Thai, Japanese, Tibetan, and others — which are separate institutions with their own gates.
Cycle rickshaws and e-rickshaws cover town distances. Agree the fare before you sit down. There is no need for a package tour to enter the temple.
bullets: Nearest air and rail: Gaya, then a short prepaid taxi
The temple compound and the national monasteries are different sites
Walk or use a rickshaw between monasteries rather than hiring a car for every lane
Keep small cash; card payment is uneven in town

bestTime.intro: The cooler, drier months are kinder for long sitting outdoors. Festivals change the character of the compound.
paragraphs: October to March is the usual season: cooler mornings and clearer skies. April and May are very hot; the monsoon from June into September floods fields and slows roads.
The Buddha Jayanti / Vesak season and other full-moon observances fill the compound with pilgrims. That is a meaningful time to visit and a poor time to expect silence.
bullets: Best weather: October–March
Hottest: April–May — go at opening
Full-moon and Jayanti days are pilgrimage peaks, not quiet museum hours

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: The brick temple is Gupta-period in form, restored later, on a site of much older devotion. This guide does not pin the tower to a single foundation day.
Phone and camera rules at the gate have been strict in some seasons. Obey the check you meet that morning.
Tout tickets and “mandatory guide” claims at the gate are not committee policy.
The Bodhi tree is a successor tree in devotional tradition. Speak of it that way.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple
summary: Varanasi’s Jyotirlinga temple to Shiva — free general darshan through the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, with optional paid aarti only on the trust’s own portal.

body: Kashi Vishwanath is the Shiva temple at the centre of old Varanasi, counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas. The trust dates the present temple building to 1780 and Maharani Ahilyabai Holkar. The devotion at this site is older than that building.

Most visitors now approach through the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, the widened route between the ghats and the temple. General darshan is free. The sanctum is small, the queue is the visit, and phones are often left in lockers before the inner gate.

Sugam Darshan, Mangala aarti, and Rudrabhishek are optional paid services. The Shri Kashi Vishwanath Temple Trust sells them on shrikashivishwanath.org. A priest in the lane selling the “same” aarti is not the trust.
highlights: Free general darshan; paid aarti only on the trust portal
Approach via the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor from the river side
Security, lockers, and a slow queue
Pair with a separate, unhurried walk on the ghats

visit.intro: Enter for darshan without buying anything. Add an aarti only if you have booked it on the official portal.
visit.hours: The trust publishes darshan breaks around midday aarti and evening rituals. A widely posted pattern is morning darshan, a pause for bhog, afternoon and evening darshan, then a late pause for shringar. Read the day’s schedule on the portal before you promise someone a sunset slot.
visit.tickets: General darshan: free. Sugam Darshan (assisted, shorter queue) and named aartis are paid on the official portal. Prices on that site change; the trust’s own FAQ has described general entry as free and special darshan as a paid option.
visit.dress: The trust does not impose a detailed dress code and does ask for decent clothes. Shoulders and knees covered will not be wrong. Leather belts and shoes are commonly restricted — use the lockers and the shoe stands.
visit.duration: One and a half to three hours once you are in the corridor queue. The ghats before or after are a separate hour.
visit.access: The corridor is broad. The temple interior is tight, stepped in places, and crowded. People who cannot stand in a slow queue should look at Sugam Darshan on the official site rather than forcing the free line.
tips: Book aarti only at shrikashivishwanath.org — not via a WhatsApp number in a guesthouse.
Put the phone away before the inner gate; many visits require it to be deposited.
Mangala aarti is in the small hours. Only go if the portal lists it for that date.
Keep the ghat walk and the temple queue as two plans so a delay in one does not wreck the other.
visit.ticketsNote: General darshan is free. Optional Sugam Darshan and aarti are paid only on this trust portal. Ignore lane-side “official booking” desks.

etiquette.intro: You are in a working temple, in a queue of people who have come to stand before the linga.
bullets: Do not touch the linga, the priests’ tray, or offerings.
Keep the phone silent and pocketed once you are past the locker point.
Do not push to the rail for a longer look; the line moves past the sanctum.
Ask before photographing anyone. Inside the sanctum, assume photography is forbidden unless a sign says otherwise.
Refuse unsolicited “guides” who attach themselves in the corridor.

gettingThere.intro: The temple is in the old city above the Ganges, reached on foot from the corridor gates or from Godowlia.
paragraphs: Varanasi’s airport (VNS) and the railway stations are a taxi or autorickshaw ride from the old city. Vehicles stop outside the lanes. The last stretch is on foot through the corridor or the market.
Dashashwamedh Ghat is the famous nearby ghat, not the temple door. Follow corridor signs for Kashi Vishwanath rather than a boatman’s shortcut.
bullets: Fly into VNS or arrive by rail, then an auto to the old-city edge
Use the corridor entrance, not a random alley a stranger insists on
Boat rides on the river are a separate hire — agree the price on the ghat
Wear shoes you can take off quickly

bestTime.intro: Cool months are easier in the marble queue. Festival weeks are when Varanasi is most itself, and most full.
paragraphs: November to February is the comfortable season. March to June is hot, and the queue has little shade. The monsoon is dramatic on the river and slow in the lanes.
Dev Deepawali, Mahashivaratri, and the month of Shravan draw very large crowds. Go at opening on those days or choose an ordinary Tuesday if you want a shorter wait.
bullets: Best weather: November–February
Major Shiva festivals fill the corridor for days
Early morning is cooler and closer to Mangala aarti, if you are booked or simply walking in

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: The present building is the Holkar temple of 1780. The Jyotirlinga tradition is older than that building.
Aarti prices and darshan breaks are whatever the trust portal says this week.
Pickpockets work the lanes outside. Use the lockers for what you can.
The corridor is a public approach, not a place to set up a photo shoot of worshippers.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
summary: The head Inari shrine, at the foot of a mountain of vermilion torii — free to enter, and a real walk if you go beyond the first tunnel of gates.

quickFacts.typicalVisit: 1 hour at the shrine; 2–3 hours if you climb

body: Fushimi Inari Taisha is the head shrine of Inari, at the southern edge of Kyoto. The shrine’s own account dates its founding to 711. Foxes are the deity’s messengers here, which is why the grounds are full of fox statues. They are not a zoo and not a petting stop.

There is no admission fee and no ticket. The famous Senbon torii — the densely packed vermilion gates — start behind the main sanctuary and continue up Mount Inari. The lower tunnel is the photograph. The mountain above it is the visit.

The paths stay open around the clock. The shrine office does not. At night the gates are quieter and the stone is uneven; bring a light if you go after dusk, and do not treat the mountain as a lit park.
highlights: JR Inari Station is beside the shrine
Torii continue to the summit — about two hours round trip
New Year and the 1st of each month are packed

visit.intro: Walk up as far as you mean to, then turn around. There is no ticket window to miss and no need to buy one from a booth nearby.
visit.hours: The mountain paths are open day and night. The shrine office is typically open in the daytime (commonly about 8:30am–4:30pm). Confirm anything you need from the office — goshuin, formal prayers — on inari.jp.
visit.tickets: Admission is free. Torii along the trail are donated by businesses and households; that is a shrine practice, not a visitor ticket.
visit.dress: Everyday modest clothes. You will climb. Wear shoes with grip; the upper paths are dirt, root, and stone, and they are slick after rain.
visit.duration: Forty minutes if you only walk the lower gates and the main hall. Two to three hours for a return trip toward the summit, with a pause at Yotsutsuji.
visit.access: The lower shrine is gentle. The mountain is a continuous climb with few flat stretches. It is not a step-free site. Turn around whenever you need to; the path is the same coming down.
tips: Stand to the side of a torii, not in the middle of the gate.
Let people pass on the trail. Do not stop in the narrowest tunnels for a long pose.
Carry water. Vending machines thin out as you climb.
If you want a formal prayer or a goshuin, arrive while the office is open.
visit.ticketsNote: Admission is free. There is no ticket for the torii paths. The shrine asks visitors to keep the mountain a place of worship.

etiquette.intro: The whole mountain is shrine ground, including the parts that look like a hiking trail.
bullets: Bow lightly at the torii and walk to the side.
Do not eat while walking through the gate tunnels.
Do not climb on fox statues, gates, or the clusters of miniature torii.
Keep voices down near the main sanctuary and the smaller shrines higher up.
Take your rubbish down with you. The mountain is not staffed like a theme park.

gettingThere.intro: The simplest arrival in Kyoto is the train that stops at the shrine door.
paragraphs: JR Nara Line to Inari Station: two stops, about five minutes from Kyoto Station, and the shrine gate is immediately outside. Keihan Fushimi-Inari Station is a few minutes’ walk to the west.

The shrine asks visitors to come by train. The car parks fill, and they are for worshippers. A taxi from downtown Kyoto is straightforward if you miss the train, and unnecessary if you are already at Kyoto Station.
bullets: JR Inari, next to the gate — the reliable way in
Keihan Fushimi-Inari is the alternative, a short walk west
Do not count on parking
The summit is a hike, not a second train stop

bestTime.intro: Go early, or go knowing you will share the lower gates with everyone else.
paragraphs: The hour after dawn is when the lower torii belong to people who are actually walking. By mid-morning the first tunnel is a queue with cameras.
The first days of January, and the 1st of each month, are festival-level crowds. Weekday afternoons in winter are quieter, and the mountain is colder than central Kyoto.
bullets: Best: sunrise or a winter weekday
Avoid if you want quiet: New Year and the 1st of the month
After rain the upper path needs shoes with grip, not smooth soles

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: The year 711 is the shrine’s traditional founding, as the shrine itself states it.
Night walking is allowed and unlit in stretches. It is a poor idea in dress shoes or without a light.
Souvenir stalls at the base are not the shrine office.
Read the visitor requests on inari.jp before you fly a drone or stage a shoot. The answer is no.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Sultan Ahmed Mosque (Blue Mosque)
summary: Sultan Ahmed I’s imperial mosque opposite Hagia Sophia — six minarets, Iznik tile, and free entry between the prayers.

body: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque, called the Blue Mosque for the Iznik tiles inside, faces the Hippodrome in Sultanahmet. Sultan Ahmed I commissioned it; Sedefkar Mehmed Agha, trained in the line of Mimar Sinan, built it between 1609 and 1616. It is a working mosque, not a museum with a turnstile.

Entry is free. Donations toward upkeep are voluntary and belong in the boxes provided, not in a stranger’s hand at the door. Visitor hours sit around the five daily prayers, and the building closes to sightseers while people are praying.
Hagia Sophia is across the square and follows different rules, including a paid visitor route. A ticket for one is not a ticket for the other. Plan them as two visits.
highlights: Closed to visitors during prayers, and on Friday until early afternoon
Shawls available if your clothes are not modest enough
A separate visit from Hagia Sophia

visit.intro: Come between prayers, with shoulders and knees covered, and use the visitor entrance rather than walking into the men’s prayer lines.
visit.hours: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque preservation association publishes visitor hours of about 8:30am–7:00pm in the summer season (1 April–30 September) and 8:30am–5:00pm in winter (1 October–31 March). Last entry is earlier than closing. On Fridays, tourist entry starts in the early afternoon, commonly 14:30. The mosque also closes around the noon and afternoon prayers.
visit.tickets: There is no ticket. Anyone selling a Blue Mosque ticket outside is not selling an official product.
visit.dress: Cover shoulders, chest, and knees before you reach the door. Women cover their hair inside. Bare legs and sleeveless tops are turned away or lent a wrap. Shoes come off; use the plastic bags or racks so you are not carrying dirty soles against your clothes.
visit.duration: Forty-five to seventy-five minutes for the courtyard and the interior. Longer if you wait out a prayer closure.
visit.access: The courtyard is broad. The interior is carpeted and level once shoes are off, with some steps at entrances. Strollers are commonly stopped at the door. Ask an attendant if you need a step-free entrance rather than guessing.
tips: If a prayer is about to start, wait in the courtyard instead of arguing at the rope.
Use the wrap desk if you are unsure about dress. It is faster than walking back to the hotel.
Keep the visit and Hagia Sophia as two timed plans.
Recheck sultanahmetcami.org the week you go — Friday rules are the ones that catch people.
visit.ticketsNote: Entry is free. This page is the mosque preservation association’s visitor guide. Do not pay a third party for admission.

etiquette.intro: Worshippers are the reason the doors close. Visitors fit around them.
bullets: Speak quietly. The dome carries sound further than you expect.
Stay inside the visitor area when a rope or an attendant marks the prayer space.
Do not photograph people while they are praying, and do not use flash.
Smoking is not allowed in the courtyard.
Put shoes back on outside, not while blocking the door.

gettingThere.intro: Sultanahmet is the tourist centre of the old city, and the mosque is the landmark you can already see from the tram.
paragraphs: Take the T1 tram to Sultanahmet and walk a few minutes uphill toward the six minarets. The mosque sits on the south side of the old Hippodrome; Hagia Sophia is on the north side of the square.
Taxis can drop you at the square. They cannot help once prayer closure has started. Build the walk into the plan so you are not late for a Friday afternoon opening.
bullets: T1 tram, Sultanahmet stop
The mosque, Hagia Sophia, and the Hippodrome are three separate visits in one neighbourhood
Istanbulkart covers the tram; buy it before you need it
There is no useful parking at the door

bestTime.intro: A weekday morning, not Friday noon, and not the hour a prayer is called.
paragraphs: Arrive near opening on a Monday to Thursday. The courtyard is already busy by late morning in summer, and cruise-ship groups come in waves.
Friday is a congregational day. Tourist entry waits until early afternoon, and even then the building feels like a mosque first, which is what it is.
bullets: Best: weekday right after opening
Skip as a casual visit: Friday before mid-afternoon, and the half hour around each prayer
Ramadan evenings are beautiful and crowded — the courtyard fills for iftar

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: Construction ran from 1609 to 1616 under Sultan Ahmed I. Visitors are guests of a working mosque.
Hours above follow the mosque association’s published seasonal windows. Confirm them on the official guide before a tight connection.
A “skip the line” pass is meaningless at a free mosque. It is a sales pitch.
The interior is an active prayer hall. Sit on the carpet only where visitors are clearly allowed to pause.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Westminster Abbey
summary: The coronation church of England — a working Gothic abbey beside Parliament, with paid sightseeing tickets and free worship.

body: Westminster Abbey is a living church of the Church of England and the place of coronations since 1066. The present Gothic building was begun in 1245 under Henry III. It also holds the tombs of kings and of people buried in Poets’ Corner, and it sits directly beside the Palace of Westminster.

Sightseeing is paid and timed. Worship is not. Regular services are free and do not use a sightseeing ticket; they are also not a back door for a tour. Buy entry only from the Abbey’s own ticket store.
State occasions close the church with little public notice. A ticket is not a guarantee if Parliament Square is shut for a ceremony. A sightseeing ticket is not an invitation to a state service.
highlights: Paid timed entry for sightseeing; services are free
Security screening and a modest dress expectation
The Abbey can close at short notice for state occasions

visit.intro: Book a timed sightseeing ticket if you want to walk the church. Come to a service if you want to pray. They are different doors in the same building.
visit.hours: Sightseeing hours change by season and are posted on westminster-abbey.org. Last entry is earlier than closing. Service times are on the same site and are not sightseeing slots.
visit.tickets: Buy sightseeing tickets from tickets.westminster-abbey.org. The Abbey states that tickets bought through unofficial sellers can be refused, and that services are free of charge. Prices change; read the live tariff rather than a saved screenshot.
visit.dress: Modest clothing, shoulders covered, as for any working church. Large backpacks slow you at security and are awkward in the aisles — leave them at the hotel.
visit.duration: Ninety minutes to two and a half hours. The audio guide is worth using; the chapels are dense with tombs and easy to walk past.
visit.access: Security is airport-style. Much of the main floor is step-aware stone. Some chapels and the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries involve stairs or a lift with limited capacity. Ask the visitor desk about step-free routes when you arrive.
tips: Book ahead in summer, at Easter, and around Christmas. Door sales are limited.
Arrive for the time on the ticket. Late arrivals are helped when they can be, not guaranteed a slot.
Do not block a procession or a funeral. Both still happen here.
St Margaret’s Church next door is not included just because you can see it. Check its own notice.
visit.ticketsNote: Westminster Abbey’s own ticket store for sightseeing. Services are free and are listed separately on westminster-abbey.org. Prices change — confirm before you pay.

etiquette.intro: People are buried here, and people are still praying here. Both facts outrank a photograph.
bullets: Silence the phone. Speak at the level of the person beside you, not the person across the nave.
Do not climb on tombs, gates, or the Cosmati pavement.
During a service, put the camera away.
Follow stewards if a chapel is closed for prayer or for conservation.
Flash is unwelcome. Tripods are not allowed.

gettingThere.intro: The Abbey is in Westminster, between Parliament Square and a pair of Tube stations.
paragraphs: Westminster station (Jubilee, District, Circle) and St James’s Park station (District, Circle) are both a short walk. Leave extra time when Parliament Square is busy or closed.
There is no visitor car park. River buses to Westminster Pier are a pleasant approach and still end in the same security queue.
bullets: Tube: Westminster or St James’s Park
Allow a buffer when a demonstration or state visit has closed the square
Cloisters, the Chapter House, and the garden are sometimes on the same ticket and sometimes on a shorter clock — read that day’s entry times
The Palace of Westminster next door is a separate visit with its own tickets

bestTime.intro: A weekday morning slot, booked, beats a Saturday walk-up.
paragraphs: May to September, Easter, and the days around Christmas are the crowded months. The Abbey itself warns that door sales may stop and waits grow.
Weekday openings outside school holidays are the calmest sightseeing. Evensong, when you are there to attend it, is a better reason to come late than a hope of slipping in free.
bullets: Book: any summer day, and any day near a state occasion
Calmer: winter weekdays
If the Abbey announces a closure, the ticket office — not a hotel — is who moves your visit

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: Coronations since 1066 and a Gothic church begun in 1245 are the historical frame. Sightseeing is not a ceremony.
A sightseeing ticket is not valid as a way to skip security or to attend a closed ceremony.
Photography rules can tighten with no notice when a service is underway.
Resellers using the Abbey’s name are a known problem. The only sightseeing checkout is the Abbey’s own store.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Mont-Saint-Michel Abbey
summary: The abbey on the tidal rock in Normandy — the village is free to enter, the abbey is a paid national monument, and the bay is not a beach to wander.

body: Mont-Saint-Michel is a tidal island in Normandy, crowned by a medieval abbey. The foundation is traditionally tied to the early 8th century and Saint Aubert; the church you walk through is Romanesque and Gothic, built up over later centuries. It is one of the first French sites inscribed by UNESCO.

The village streets are a commune. They are free, steep, and open without a ticket. The abbey above them is a national monument run with the Centre des monuments nationaux. Abbey entry is timed and paid, with concessions that you claim from the official tariff, not from a shop on the causeway.
The bay around the rock moves. Tides come in faster than a casual walk back across the sand. Cross on the causeway or the shuttle. Go onto the sands only with an accredited guide.
highlights: Village free; abbey ticketed via the official monument site
Causeway or shuttle from the mainland car parks — do not drive to the rock
Tides are a safety issue, not a backdrop
Last abbey entry is an hour before closing

visit.intro: Decide before you arrive whether you are walking the village only or also entering the abbey. Only the abbey needs a ticket.
visit.hours: The abbey is typically open 9:00am–7:00pm from 1 May to 31 August and 9:30am–6:00pm from 1 September to 30 April, and closed on 1 January, 1 May, and 25 December. Last entry is one hour before closing. The village has no such gate.
visit.tickets: Buy abbey tickets from the abbey’s own site, which sells through the Centre des monuments nationaux. Individual prices published for 2026 were €16 in the high season and €13 in the low season; concessions, including many visitors under 26, are listed on that page and change. Bring ID if you are claiming one.
visit.dress: The abbey is a church as well as a monument. Modest dress is enough. Wear shoes you can stand in on cobbles and stairs. The village is a climb, not a stroll.
visit.duration: Half a day for the shuttle, the village, and the abbey. A full day if you also walk with a guide on the flats.
visit.access: Streets are steep, cobbled, and crowded. The abbey visit includes many stairs. Minors must be with an adult inside the abbey. Dogs are not admitted, including in a carrier. There is no cloakroom for large luggage inside the monument.
tips: Load the e-ticket on your phone before you reach the rock. The network at the door is poor.
Do not walk the bay without an accredited guide. Fog and tide together are how people get into trouble.
Eat in the village if you want, knowing the main street is priced for a captive audience. Bring water either way.
Free-entry days exist, including some first Sundays in winter. Read the abbey page for that month instead of assuming.
visit.ticketsNote: Official abbey page for hours, tariffs, and the Centre des monuments nationaux booking link. The village below the abbey is free. Confirm the current price before you pay.

etiquette.intro: The abbey is still a sacred building inside a national monument. The village is still someone’s street.
bullets: Keep to the side of the Grande Rue so residents and handcarts can pass.
Inside the abbey, voices low, hats off in the church, no eating.
Do not climb parapets or lean out over the bay for a photograph.
Do not scratch initials into stone. The monument staff do pursue it.
Birds and the tide are not entertainment. Do not feed either.

gettingThere.intro: You park on the mainland and cross the causeway. Cars do not go onto the island.
paragraphs: The visitor area and car parks are south of the rock, off the causeway. From there, walk or take the Passeur shuttle. Both end at the gates, and both can queue in July.
Trains serve Pontorson or Rennes, with a bus connection onward. If a hotel offers a “drop at the abbey door,” it means the mainland shuttle point, not the Gothic steps.
bullets: Park at the official mainland car parks, then walk or ride the shuttle
Do not follow a shortcut onto the sand because the tide “looks far”
Allow longer on summer weekends; the shuttle queue is part of the trip
Check tide times if anyone in your group plans a guided bay walk

bestTime.intro: The rock is at its best when you can see it, and at its most tiring when everyone else can too.
paragraphs: Late spring and early autumn give you the abbey without the August crush. July and August are when the Grande Rue becomes a slow single file.
Winter light on the bay is extraordinary, and some winter Sundays are free-entry days for the abbey. Wind on the west terrace is not theoretical; bring a layer.
bullets: Calmer: May–June and September–October weekdays
Hardest: weekends in July and August, and French school holidays
Storm days can close terraces even when the ticket is valid

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: The 8th-century foundation is a traditional date. It is not a ceremony a visitor attends.
Tariffs and free Sundays are whatever the abbey publishes for the current season.
A ticket for the abbey is not a permit to walk the bay.
E-tickets that never arrive should go to the monument’s own customer service, not to a reseller who met you in the car park.

name: Temple of Heaven
summary: The Ming and Qing altar where emperors ritually addressed Heaven — now a public park, with a separate ticket for the halls.

body: The Temple of Heaven is the imperial altar complex southeast of the Forbidden City, where Ming and Qing emperors offered state rites to Heaven and prayed for the harvest. The park is round to the north and square to the south, the old “heaven round, earth square” plan, with a long raised Danbi Bridge between the Circular Mound and the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests.

It is a park and a monument, not a neighbourhood temple with a congregation. You will see people exercising in the cypress groves at dawn. You will not find a visitor rite to join, and SanctaWay will not invent one. The Hall of Prayer standing today was rebuilt in 1889 after lightning destroyed its predecessor.

Two payments matter. A park ticket lets you into the gardens. A through-ticket adds the Hall of Prayer, the Echo Wall, and the Circular Mound. Beijing’s municipal parks office sells both on its own platform and at the gate. It has said plainly that third-party sites are not authorized.
highlights: UNESCO imperial altar, now a public park
Park ticket and hall through-ticket are different
Buy only via Beijing’s official parks platform or the gate window
Main halls often closed on Mondays

visit.intro: Buy the through-ticket if you want to go inside the halls. A garden ticket stops you at their doors.
visit.hours: In the high season (1 April–31 October) the park opens around 6:00am and closes at night; in the low season it opens around 6:30am. The halls open later, about 8:00am, and stop entry in the late afternoon. The park’s own site lists Monday closures for the main halls, with exceptions on statutory holidays and in a midsummer window. Read tiantanpark.com for the week you are there.
visit.tickets: Official online sales are the “Visiting Beijing Parks” platform at bjgyol.com.cn, which is the municipal parks channel and can be switched to English. Foreign visitors can also buy at the gate’s service window with a passport; cards and cash are accepted there. Do not use Klook, Viator, or a hotel desk that cannot name this channel.
visit.dress: Ordinary modest clothes. You will walk a long way on open marble and under cypress. A hat and water matter more than formal dress. Quiet voices inside the halls.
visit.duration: Two to three hours for the north–south axis without rushing. Longer if you add the park’s outer groves.
visit.access: The axis is long and exposed. There are steps up to the Hall of Prayer and the Circular Mound. Ask at the east or south gate about step-free routes if stairs are a problem; do not assume every terrace has a ramp.
tips: Enter at Tiantan Dongmen (east) from Line 5 if you want the shortest walk from the metro.
Go to the halls when they open, then walk the park. The groves at dawn are locals, not a show.
At the Echo Wall, speak; do not shout, and do not scratch the brick.
If the English online form rejects a foreign phone number, use the gate window rather than a reseller.
visit.ticketsNote: Beijing’s official municipal-parks ticket platform, which includes the Temple of Heaven. The city states that third-party sellers are not authorized. Gate windows sell the same tickets with a passport. Hours and prices: tiantanpark.com.

etiquette.intro: The buildings were made for an emperor’s rite. They are quiet interiors now. Keep them that way.
bullets: Do not climb railings or step onto protected marble that is roped off.
Do not carve, chalk, or scratch the Echo Wall. Staff do stop people.
Inside the halls, no flash and no livestream at full volume.
The dawn exercise groups were here first. Walk around them.
Smoking is banned in the halls and a bad idea under cypress in dry months.

gettingThere.intro: The park is large. The gate you choose decides how far you walk before you see a hall.
paragraphs: Metro Line 5, Tiantan Dongmen, is the practical entrance and lands you at the east gate. Line 8’s Tianqiao area and several buses serve the west and south sides if you are coming from Qianmen.
Taxis can use the named gates. Give the gate, not only “Tiantan,” or you may be dropped on the wrong side of a very long wall.
bullets: Metro: Tiantan Dongmen, Line 5, east gate
Name the gate to a taxi driver
The Danbi Bridge between the two altars is a long exposed walk — bring water
Audio guides rented at the gates are the park’s own; a person who approaches you inside is not

bestTime.intro: Come early for the park, and come on a day the halls are actually open.
paragraphs: April and October are the comfortable months. Summer is hot on the marble terraces; winter is beautiful and very cold in the wind across the Circular Mound.
Monday is the day most likely to disappoint if you wanted the interior of the Hall of Prayer. The gardens may still be open when the halls are not.
bullets: Best walking weather: April–May and September–October
Check Monday hall closures before you buy a through-ticket for that day
Dawn is for a park walk; hall interiors start later in the morning

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: These were imperial altars. There is no living congregation and no visitor rite to join.
The 1889 date belongs to the rebuilt Hall of Prayer, not to a modern rite.
A reseller QR code is not a Beijing parks ticket. If the gate cannot scan it, you will buy again.
Prices move between high season and low season. Read them on tiantanpark.com the week you go.

name: Lotus Temple (Baháʼí House of Worship)
summary: The Baháʼí House of Worship in Delhi, a white lotus in marble — free to enter, closed on Mondays, and open to people of every faith.

body: The Lotus Temple is the Baháʼí House of Worship for the Indian subcontinent, in Kalkaji, south Delhi. The National Spiritual Assembly of the Baháʼís of India opened it for public worship in 1986. The building is the work of architect Fariborz Sahba: twenty-seven marble petals, set in gardens and pools.

It is not a Hindu temple, a Buddhist vihara, or a mosque, though people of those faiths are welcome. Baháʼí houses of worship have no clergy, no sermons, and no images. The prayer hall is for quiet reading and for short services drawn from many scriptures. Nothing is asked of a visitor except quiet.
Entry is free. The house is closed on Mondays. On other days the official visiting hours are 8:30am to 5:00pm, with brief prayer services at 10:00, 12:00, 3:00, and 5:00.
highlights: Prayer hall for silence, not a ritual you can book
Metro: Kalkaji Mandir, a short walk
Groups of ten or more should request a weekday appointment

visit.intro: Come to sit quietly. There is nothing to buy to get in, and nothing you are required to perform once you are inside.
visit.hours: Tuesday to Sunday, 8:30am–5:00pm. Closed Monday. Prayer services last about ten to fifteen minutes at 10:00am, 12:00pm, 3:00pm, and 5:00pm. During a service the hall doors stay closed until the reading ends. The hall may also close when it is overcrowded or in heavy rain.
visit.tickets: Entry is free. The house is maintained by voluntary Baháʼí contributions, not by an admission charge. Anyone selling a Lotus Temple ticket is not selling an official product.
visit.dress: Modest clothing, shoulders covered, clothes you can sit on the floor in if the benches are full. Shoes come off before the prayer hall and stay in the racks.
visit.duration: An hour to ninety minutes, including the gardens. The hall itself is a short, quiet sit unless you stay for a service.
visit.access: Gardens and the approach are broad. The prayer hall is entered barefoot. Ask the information staff about step-free access rather than assuming every petal walkway is a ramp. On crowded Sundays the hall may simply be full.
tips: Kalkaji Mandir metro (Violet and Magenta lines) is about a five-minute walk. Okhla NSIC on the Magenta line is the other nearby stop.
If you want a service, arrive ten minutes early. You will not be let out mid-reading.
Groups of ten or more: use the appointment form on the official site at least three days ahead. Weekends and public holidays are not appointment days.
The gardens are part of the visit. The prayer hall is not a backdrop for a loud video.
visit.ticketsNote: Official visitor page of the Baháʼí House of Worship, New Delhi. Entry is free. The house is closed on Mondays.

etiquette.intro: The only thing asked of you inside is quiet, and that you not turn someone else’s prayer into content.
bullets: Silence the phone before the shoe racks.
Do not chant, preach, or perform another religion’s rite in the hall.
Follow the photography signs. If the hall is posted as no photography, put the camera away.
Stay seated until a service ends. The doors are closed on purpose.
Do not pick flowers or step into the pools.

gettingThere.intro: Kalkaji is in south Delhi. The metro is the reliable way; a taxi is the backup in traffic.
paragraphs: From New Delhi station, the official guidance is the Yellow line toward Central Secretariat, then the Violet line to Kalkaji Mandir, and a short walk. From the airport, the Magenta line reaches Okhla NSIC, also a short walk.
Autos and app taxis can drop you at the gate on Bahapur. Say “Lotus Temple, Kalkaji,” not only “Baháʼí,” or you may be taken to a different address.
bullets: Metro: Kalkaji Mandir or Okhla NSIC, then a five-minute walk
There is public parking opposite the main gate
Allow more time on Sunday, when Delhi treats the gardens as an outing
The house is not inside Old Delhi; do not combine it on foot with Chandni Chowk

bestTime.intro: A weekday morning is the building as it was meant to be entered. Sunday is a crowd.
paragraphs: Tuesday to Friday mornings are calm, and the marble reads clearly in early light. Sundays and public holidays fill the gardens and can close the hall once capacity is reached.
Delhi summers are extreme by late morning. Winter mornings are pleasant. The monsoon can close the hall for rain even when you have crossed the city to be there.
bullets: Best: weekday at opening
Closed: every Monday
Sunday afternoon is the most likely time to find the hall full

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: Opened for public worship in 1986, in the community’s own wording. It is not a Hindu temple, and no puja is performed for visitors.
Service times and Monday closure are published on bahaihouseofworship.in. Recheck them before a group visit.
There is no official ticket. Do not pay one.
Heavy rain and overcrowding can close the hall on a day the gardens stay open.
SanctaWay is informational; it does not sell tickets or grant access.

name: Chichén Itzá
summary: The great Maya city of Yucatán — El Castillo, the ball court, and the cenote — entered only with the on-site INAH ticket, and not by climbing the pyramids.

body: Chichén Itzá is a Maya city in the Yucatán, occupied across the Classic and Postclassic periods and dominated today by El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcán. Around it sit the Great Ball Court, the Temple of the Warriors, and the Sacred Cenote. It has been a UNESCO site since 1988.

It is an archaeological zone under INAH, the national institute of anthropology and history, not a working temple and not a ceremony you can buy. Climbing the pyramids is prohibited. Do not buy a private rite or a “shaman package.”

Admission is a single on-site ticket at the CATVI visitor window, combining the INAH fee and the Yucatán state fee. INAH’s own notices say to buy it there. A wristband from a Cancún hotel desk is not a substitute.
highlights: Buy the day ticket only at the on-site CATVI window

visit.intro: Pay at the gate window, then walk. Do not pay a resort rep, a roadside flagger, or an equinox package for the same entry.
visit.hours: INAH lists the zone as open every day from 8:00am to 5:00pm, with last tickets around 4:00pm and clearing of the site after that. Equinox weekends add crowd controls; the institute publishes those plans separately.
visit.tickets: Buy at the CATVI window inside the visitor centre. INAH has published a combined foreign-visitor price and lower prices for Mexican visitors, with free entry on Sundays for Mexican nationals and foreign residents who can prove it, and weekday exemptions for Yucatán residents and for several concession categories. Numbers change. The window, not a blog, is the price list that matters. There is no official skip-the-line reseller.
visit.dress: Light clothes, a hat, and shoes you can walk in. The site is bare limestone, with little shade. Shoulders can burn in an hour. Rain turns the stone slick.
visit.duration: Three to four hours if you walk as far as the cenote and still leave time to look at the ball court. Less if you only circle El Castillo and get back on a bus.
visit.access: Main paths are broad and partly ramped, and wheelchairs can reach the central plazas. Side paths are rocky. You cannot climb El Castillo or the other structures. There is little shade and almost no seating.
tips: Arrive at opening. Tour buses from Cancún and the Riviera land in force in the late morning.
Bring water in. Drink it. The sun here is the main hazard.
Use only licensed site staff for a guide. Agree the price before you walk.
The evening sound-and-light show, when it is running, is a separate state event and a separate ticket. It is not included in the INAH day ticket.
visit.ticketsNote: Official INAH page for the zone. Admission is sold at the Chichén Itzá CATVI window, not online through unauthorized platforms. Confirm the day’s price at that window.

etiquette.intro: These are archaeological structures. Standing on them, or staging a rite on them, is not part of a visit.
bullets: Do not climb pyramids, the ball-court walls, or roped staircases.
Do not touch carved panels or lean on them for a photo.
Drones need prior written permission from INAH. Assume you do not have it.
Vendors inside the site are licensed; a person who offers a “spiritual ceremony” at the cenote is not your guide.
Talk at a normal volume. The plazas echo, and sound carries.

gettingThere.intro: The site is inland, between Valladolid and Mérida, about two kilometres from the town of Pisté.
paragraphs: From Mérida it is roughly 115 kilometres east, a day trip by ADO bus or by car via Pisté. From Cancún or the Riviera it is a much longer day; an organized coach is common and still drops you at the same official ticket window.
There is no train-to-the-door in ordinary use for this visit. Taxis from Valladolid are a practical middle distance. Agree the return before you walk in, or you will negotiate in the heat at 3pm.
bullets: By road from Mérida, Valladolid, or the Caribbean coast
Pisté is the service town; the gate is a short ride further
Buy nothing that claims to replace the CATVI ticket
Confirm the return bus before you start walking the site

bestTime.intro: The dry season is kinder. The equinox is famous and packed, and the pyramid is still not for climbing.
paragraphs: November to April is drier and slightly cooler. May to September is hot, humid, and subject to heavy afternoon rain. Go early in every season.

Around the March and September equinoxes, people come for the serpent-shaped shadow on El Castillo’s north stair. INAH runs a crowd operation on those days. It is a public viewing, not a ritual you join, and it is the worst day to expect a quiet hour.
bullets: Best weather: the dry winter and early spring
Go at 8:00am in every month
Equinox days are a managed crowd — read INAH’s bulletin if you insist on that date

notes.intro: 注意事項 · Verify before visit
bullets: Chichén Itzá is an archaeological zone. Climbing is closed. No visitor rite is offered here.
Ticket prices and Sunday exemptions change by federal and state tariff. Pay at the CATVI window.
Heat illness is the common emergency. Water, a hat, and an early start prevent it.
Professional cameras, tripods, and drones need INAH permits arranged before you travel.
